items.title: The Domesday Book recorded almost every pig in England
items.claim: William I commissioned the Domesday survey in 1085, completed 1086. How detailed was it?

options.text: It listed only the major landholders and royal manors
It recorded landholders, ploughs, mills, fishponds, livestock and even individual peasants down to the level of swineherds — over 13,000 places
It was a list of military obligations only

items.reveal_title: Not one ox or cow escaped
items.reveal:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E text) complained: 'So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land, nor indeed (it is a shame to relate but it seemed no shame to him to do) one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.'

Commissioners visited every shire, took sworn testimony, and produced the survey in around a year. The original manuscripts (Great Domesday and Little Domesday) survive at The National Archives, Kew.
items.why: Medieval government is often dismissed as primitive. Domesday is more administratively detailed than anything attempted in Europe for centuries afterwards.

items.title: Henry VIII had six wives — divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived
items.claim: What is the standard rhyme for Henry VIII's wives' fates?

options.text: 'Divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived' — Catherine of Aragon (annulled), Anne Boleyn (executed 1536), Jane Seymour (died after childbirth 1537), Anne of Cleves (annulled), Catherine Howard (executed 1542), Catherine Parr (survived him)

items.reveal_title: Six queens, three Catherines, two Annes
items.reveal:
Catherine of Aragon (m. 1509, annulled 1533, died 1536) was Henry's brother Arthur's widow. Anne Boleyn (m. 1533, executed 19 May 1536) bore Elizabeth I. Jane Seymour (m. 1536, died 24 October 1537) bore Edward VI.

Anne of Cleves (m. and annulled 1540) negotiated a comfortable settlement and lived until 1557. Catherine Howard (m. 1540, executed 13 February 1542) was perhaps 17 at marriage. Catherine Parr (m. 1543) outlived Henry (d. January 1547) and died in 1548.

The rhyme 'divorced, beheaded, died' is a 19th-century mnemonic; Tudor contemporaries did not summarise the marriages this way.
items.why: Royal personal lives can carry constitutional weight. Henry's marital sequence drove the English Reformation, the succession crisis, and ultimately the Tudor dynasty's extinction with Elizabeth I in 1603.

items.title: Naseby (1645) was won by the New Model Army
items.claim: What was the Battle of Naseby?

options.text: On 14 June 1645, Parliament's New Model Army under Sir Thomas Fairfax (with Oliver Cromwell commanding cavalry) decisively defeated Charles I's army in Northamptonshire — capturing his correspondence with foreign powers and ending hope of Royalist victory
A naval engagement in the English Channel
The first battle of the war (1642)

items.reveal:
The New Model Army had been formed by ordinance in February 1645 — the first national professional army, of around 22,000 men. Naseby was its first major test. Parliament's forces of around 14,000 defeated the king's 9,000.

The king's baggage train was captured, including his correspondence — letters showing he was negotiating with Irish Catholics and foreign Catholic powers for military aid. The 'King's Cabinet Opened' (published July 1645) destroyed remaining sympathy in Parliament.

Charles surrendered to the Scots in May 1646. He was handed to Parliament in 1647, tried for treason in January 1649, and executed on 30 January.
items.why: Single battles can decide wars. Naseby ended the Royalist field army; the king's captured letters ended any chance of negotiated settlement. The two together made the regicide of 1649 possible.
